title: Curves In Rn
notes: Open the lecture by naming the object of study as a moving point rather than a drawing. The source span is short, but it establishes the vocabulary that the whole course will reuse: parametrized curve, speed, length, arclength, tangent, and bending energy.

title: A Curve Is A Regular Map
notes: Emphasize the word regular before writing formulas. The map may pass through the same point twice, so the image alone cannot be the definition. The derivative is the diagnostic: if the velocity vector vanishes, the moving-particle description has stalled and the curve is not regular there.

title: Self-Intersection Is Not The Problem
notes: Use the figure eight as a useful surprise. At the crossing there are two different parameter values and two different velocity directions, so the local motion can still be perfectly regular. Contrast that with the cusp, where the picture may look like a curve but the speed collapses.

title: Reparametrization Changes The Clock
notes: Describe reparametrization as replacing the clock while keeping the oriented trace. The increasing map phi preserves the order of traversal, and the chain rule explains how speeds change. This prepares students to distinguish a coordinate signal from a geometric quantity.

title: Length Adds Speed Along The Clock
notes: Here the integral should be read as an accumulator. Fast portions contribute more per unit parameter time, but after a valid reparametrization the substitution rule gives the same total. The lower plot is the diagnostic: different speed profiles can produce the same length.

title: Rigid Motion Does Not Alter Length
notes: Connect the ambient geometry to the integral formula. A translation disappears after differentiation, and an orthogonal matrix preserves vector norms. This is the first instance of a recurring pattern: identify the quantity being measured, then check which transformations leave it unchanged.

title: Arclength Is The Intrinsic Coordinate
notes: Present s of t as a new ruler laid along the curve. Because regularity keeps speed positive, the arclength function increases strictly and can be inverted. The diagram shows why dense parameter samples do not mean equal geometric spacing until arclength is used.

title: Unit Speed Is A Useful Representative
notes: The arclength reparametrization produces a representative that moves one unit of distance per unit of parameter. Stress that the course will often keep arbitrary parametrizations instead, because families of curves and later surface formulas are easier to handle with invariant derivatives.

title: Differentiate With Respect To Arclength
notes: This slide turns arclength into an operator rather than a new picture. Dividing by speed asks how a quantity changes per unit distance traveled along the curve. The same idea also defines integration against ds, which weights parameter time by the speed of the curve.

title: The Unit Tangent Records Direction Only
notes: The unit tangent forgets speed and keeps direction. On a plane curve it can be drawn as arrows along the trace, while abstractly it is a map into the unit sphere. Students should inspect where the arrows rotate quickly, because that is where bending will concentrate.

title: Curvature Is Tangent Turning Per Length
notes: Move from velocity to tangent variation. For unit-speed curves, curvature is the size of dT/ds; for arbitrary parametrizations the same formula is recovered by dividing by speed. The comparison panels make clear that the same trace direction can turn slowly or sharply.

title: Bending Energy Squares The Turning
notes: Introduce bending energy as a global cost built from local tangent turning. Squaring matters because sharp turns are penalized disproportionately. This is the bridge from elementary curve geometry into the variational questions of elastic curves in the next chapter.

title: Three Calibration Examples
notes: Use the examples as calibration instruments, not as a list to memorize. A straight line has constant tangent and zero bending. A circle of radius r has constant curvature one over r. Stretching a helix changes how quickly its tangent turns per arclength.

title: Parameter Signals Versus Geometric Signals
notes: This is the conceptual checkpoint. Sampling density, parameter speed, and plotted point spacing belong to the chosen clock, while length, arclength differentiation, tangent direction, and bending energy belong to the oriented curve. The notebook checks are designed to expose exactly this distinction.

title: Notebook Checks As Mathematical Evidence
notes: Tie the lecture back to the assigned notebook. The computational artifacts are not ornamental; they test the chapter claims. Speed stays positive for regular examples, length agrees after reparametrization, arclength reconstruction has unit speed, and circle bending matches the expected radius law.

title: Recap: From Motion To Energy
notes: Close with the dependency chain. Start with a regular map, compute speed, accumulate arclength, normalize velocity into the unit tangent, and measure how the tangent turns. That chain is the small engine that later drives elastica, space curves, and Willmore surfaces.
